propositions.text: The applicant is a Chinese citizen who claimed refugee protection in Canada in 2010 based on fear of persecution as a Christian.
propositions.quote: The applicant, Zhi Qiang He, is a citizen of the People’s Republic of China. He claimed refugee protection shortly after entering Canada in September 2010 on the basis of his fear of persecution in China as a Christian.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the applicant's claim in 2013 but it was set aside on judicial review in 2015 and a new hearing ordered.
propositions.quote: His claim was rejected by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada in September 2013 but in January 2015 this determination was set aside on judicial review and a new hearing was ordered.

propositions.text: The new hearing was held in December 2017 and the member rejected the claim and found it manifestly unfounded.
propositions.quote: That hearing took place on December 5, 2017. For reasons delivered orally on the same day, the member rejected the claim and also found that it was manifestly unfounded.

propositions.text: The applicant now applies for judicial review of the 2017 decision under section 72(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The applicant now applies for judicial review of this decision under section 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a Chinese Christian refugee claimant whose 2017 claim rejection is now under judicial review by the applicant.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, this application for judicial review is allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The applicant completed two Personal Information Forms in 2010 and 2012 with lawyer assistance, the second containing new details.
propositions.quote: The applicant set out the grounds for his claim for protection in a Personal Information Form [PIF] completed in October 2010. A lawyer in Montreal assisted the applicant with completing the PIF. The applicant completed a second PIF in October 2012. A lawyer in Toronto assisted with this one. The second PIF included a new narrative which was substantially the same as the original one but which contained a number of details that had not been provided before.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the applicant completed two PIFs with lawyer help, the second adding new details.

propositions.text: The applicant was born in 1986 in Jiang Jing Town, Fujian Province, and worked as a hair stylist.
propositions.quote: The applicant was born in 1986 in Jiang Jing Town, Fuqing City, Fujian Province. He trained and worked as a hair stylist.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant's birth and occupation facts.

propositions.text: The applicant was introduced to Christianity by his parents in 2007, baptized in 2008, attended a state church, then his parents established a home church attended by about 40 people by 2010.
propositions.quote: According to the applicant, he was introduced to Christianity by his parents in June 2007. He was living with his parents in Jiang Jing at the time. The applicant claimed that he had been baptized in October 2008. He attended a state church with his parents for about six months but in late 2007 his parents established a church in their home. By 2010, about forty people were attending services there.

propositions.text: The applicant lived elsewhere for a time but attended the home church about once a month.
propositions.quote: The applicant was living elsewhere for a time but still attended services at his parents’ home about once a month.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the applicant's Christian background and church attendance.

propositions.text: The applicant states his parents' house church was raided by PSB in April 2010; he escaped and hid, learned his parents were arrested and PSB sought him.
propositions.quote: The applicant states that his parents’ house church was raided by 20 to 30 members of the Public Security Bureau [PSB] during a service on April 18, 2010. The applicant was present. He and another member of the congregation, Yu Xi, escaped together through the back door of the house. The applicant hid in a mountain cave until darkness fell, then went to his aunt’s home. The applicant learned that his parents and many other members of the congregation had been arrested. The applicant also learned that the PSB had gone to his home to arrest him. The PSB questioned his grandmother about his whereabouts and religious activities. The applicant also learned that the PSB were accusing him of being complicit with his parents in their religious activities and of being one of the leaders of the house church. The PSB had ordered him to report to them the next day.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states his parents' church was raided by PSB; he escaped, hid, and learned PSB sought him and arrested his parents.

propositions.text: When the applicant did not report to PSB, a Wanted Circular was posted; his aunt helped him find a smuggler to leave China to Malaysia and then to Montreal on false passports.
propositions.quote: When the applicant did not report to the PSB, they put up a Wanted Circular on the walls of buildings in his village. Concerned for his safety, the applicant’s aunt helped the applicant find a smuggler to assist him to leave the country. The applicant flew from Beijing to Malaysia on May 13, 2010, travelling on a passport provided by the smuggler. He remained in Malaysia until around June 10, 2010, when he left and travelled a route (which he could not reconstruct) to Montreal on a different false passport.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant says PSB posted a Wanted Circular; his aunt helped him flee China via smuggler to Malaysia and then Montreal on false passports.

propositions.text: In his second PIF, the applicant stated he learned his parents were sentenced to three years imprisonment in October 2010 and PSB were still looking for him.
propositions.quote: According to the narrative included in his second PIF, which he completed in October 2012, the applicant had learned recently that in October 2010 his parents had been sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. Other members of the congregation who were arrested on the day of the raid had been detained for 15 months and then released. The applicant states that he also learned recently that the PSB were still looking for him.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant's second PIF states his parents were sentenced to prison and PSB still sought him.

propositions.text: The applicant filed several documents including a Wanted Circular, Release Certificates, Notices from PSB, and letters from Reverend Ko attesting to his Christian attendance and baptism.
propositions.quote: The applicant filed several documents in support of his claim, including the following: A document in Chinese purporting to be a Wanted Circular issued by the PSB of Fuqing City dated April 22, 2010.The circular had the applicant’s photograph on it.It described the applicant and his alleged connection to his parents’ house church.It asked anyone with knowledge of the applicant to contact authorities.At the 2017 hearing of the refugee claim, the applicant testified that his grandmother had removed the circular from a wall and given it to him. Two documents in Chinese purporting to be Release Certificates for his parents issued by the PSB of Fuqing City on October 18, 2013.Both stated that their respective subjects had been “sentenced to three years’ imprisonment by the People’s Court of Fuqing City due to being involved in evil cult organization and having sabotaged Public Security order.”Both stated that “the term of imprisonment is over” and that the respective subjects are “released by the Fuqing Public Security Bureau according to Article 27 of the Criminal Procedure Law” of the People’s Republic of China. The applicant was not asked how he obtained these documents at the 2017 hearing.He stated at the 2013 hearing (a transcript of which was before the member) that a family member (it is not entirely clear who) had mailed him these documents in Canada. Two documents in Chinese purporting to be Notices issued by the Jiang Jing Branch of the PSB of Fuqing City dated October 19, 2013, to the applicant’s parents.The documents stated that each of them had been released after serving three years’ imprisonment due to their “illegal evil religious activities” and that they were required to report once a month “for the further reforming of the ideology [sic].”The applicant was not asked how he obtained these documents at the 2017 hearing.He stated at the 2013 hearing that a family member (again, it is not entirely clear who) had mailed him these documents in Canada. Two letters from Reverend David Ko of the Living Stone Assembly in Scarborough, one dated October 5, 2012, the other December 2, 2017.Reverend Ko attested to the applicant’s attendance at his church, his ability to answer “Christian questions” correctly, and his having been baptised at the Living Stone Assembly on April 16, 2011.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submitted various documents including a Wanted Circular, PSB release certificates, notices, and letters from a pastor.

propositions.text: The RPD member found the applicant's identity and citizenship established but rejected his refugee claim as he is not a genuine Christian and found the claim manifestly unfounded.
propositions.quote: The RPD member found that the applicant had established his personal identity and citizenship. The member concluded, however, that the applicant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection because he is not a genuine Christian. The member also concluded that the claim is manifestly unfounded.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant's identity established but rejected the claim as not genuine Christian and manifestly unfounded.

propositions.text: The member rejected the applicant's claim for four principal reasons.
propositions.quote: The member rejected the applicant’s claim for four principal reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD member gave four main reasons for rejecting the claim.

propositions.text: First, the member found the applicant not credible due to material inconsistencies in his accounts about baptism, presence of Mr. Xi, PSB entry, and residence at time of raid.
propositions.quote: First, the member found that the applicant was not credible because of material differences between his various accounts of events that formed the basis of his claim for protection. He omitted the fact that he had been baptised in China in October 2008 in his original PIF. He did not mention Mr. Xi in his original PIF but, according to his second PIF, Mr. Xi had pulled him out of the house after the PSB entered and the two of them fled together. In his testimony before the RPD, the applicant did not mention Mr. Xi until he was asked a direct question about him by the member. In his original PIF the applicant described members of the PSB as entering the house “without a word.” In his second PIF, he stated that he heard the PSB say “beat them” when they entered. In his testimony before the RPD, the applicant first stated that the PSB told them not to move but then said they were silent as they entered. As well, the applicant gave inconsistent or, at least, confusing accounts of where he was living at the time of the police raid.

paragraphs.summary: The member found the applicant not credible due to inconsistencies in his baptism, Mr. Xi's presence, PSB entry, and residence accounts.

propositions.text: Second, the member drew a negative credibility inference from the applicant's failure to provide documentary evidence of baptism, noting no reason he could not have obtained it.
propositions.quote: Second, the member drew a “negative credibility inference” from the fact that the applicant had failed to provide documentary evidence to corroborate his claim that he was a practicing Christian in China – in particular, documentary evidence showing that he had been baptised in 2008. The member found that there was “no reason why [the applicant] could not have gone back to his parents, or his Pastor, or somebody, to get documentary evidence to prove that he was baptized in China.”

propositions.text: The member noted the applicant said religious practices were secret but found this no longer necessary since discovery years ago.
propositions.quote: When asked directly why he had not produced any such evidence, the applicant had responded that their religious practices had been kept secret at the time. The member noted that while that may once have been so, this was no longer necessary, given that they had been discovered several years ago.

propositions.text: The member noted but did not draw conclusion from the absence of a PSB summons.
propositions.quote: The member also notes but does not expressly draw any conclusion from the fact that the applicant had not produced a PSB summons.

paragraphs.summary: The member found the applicant's failure to provide baptism evidence harmed credibility and noted secrecy no longer justified this; no conclusion on missing PSB summons.

propositions.text: Third, the member found the applicant's documentary evidence (Wanted Circular and PSB documents) fraudulent as their use is not provided for under Chinese criminal procedure.
propositions.quote: Third, the member found that the documentary evidence the applicant did produce – the Wanted Circular and the PSB documents pertaining to his parents’ detention and release – were fraudulent because their use is not provided for under Chinese criminal procedure.

paragraphs.summary: The member found the applicant's documentary evidence fraudulent as not authorized under Chinese criminal procedure.

propositions.text: Fourth, the member was not satisfied the applicant is a genuine Christian despite evidence of attendance at Living Stone Assembly.
propositions.quote: Fourth, the member was not satisfied that the applicant is a genuine Christian. The member recognized that the applicant had offered evidence of his attendance at the Living Stone Assembly but he found that this evidence was insufficient to overcome his adverse findings concerning the applicant’s credibility generally.

paragraphs.summary: The member was not convinced the applicant is a genuine Christian despite attendance evidence.

propositions.text: Based on these findings, the member dismissed the claim and found it manifestly unfounded.
propositions.quote: Based on these findings, the member dismissed the claim for protection. The member also found the claim to be manifestly unfounded.

paragraphs.summary: The member dismissed the claim and found it manifestly unfounded based on prior findings.

propositions.text: The Court reviews RPD's evidence assessment on a reasonableness standard, including credibility, genuineness of documents, and manifestly unfounded claims.
propositions.quote: It is well established that this Court reviews the RPD’s assessment of the evidence before it on a reasonableness standard (Hou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 993 at paras 6-15 [Hou]). This standard applies to the RPD’s factual findings, including its credibility determinations (Nweke v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 242 at para 17), findings concerning the genuineness of documents, and its interpretation of documentary evidence (Abdulkadir v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 318 at para 21). It also applies to the RPD’s determination that a claim is manifestly unfounded (Yuan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 755 at para 13).

paragraphs.summary: The court states it reviews RPD's evidence assessment for reasonableness, including credibility and manifestly unfounded claims.

propositions.text: The Court should show significant deference to RPD's credibility findings due to its advantage in assessing witnesses and country conditions.
propositions.quote: It is also well established that this Court should show significant deference to the RPD’s credibility findings (Su v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 518 at para 7 [Su]). This is because the RPD is well-placed to assess credibility (Aguebor v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1993), 160 NR 315, [1993] FCJ No 732 (FCA) at para 4 (QL); Hou at para 7). It has the advantage of observing the witnesses who testify and may have expertise in the subject matter that the reviewing court does not share, including with respect to country conditions (Rahal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 319 at para 42 [Rahal]; Zhou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 821 at para 58). Nevertheless, the reviewing court must ensure that the RPD’s credibility findings are reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains it must defer to RPD's credibility findings but ensure they are reasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review examines justification, transparency, intelligibility, and whether the decision is within a range of acceptable outcomes.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness review “is concerned with the reasonableness of the substantive outcome of the decision, and with the process of articulating that outcome” (Canada (Attorney General) v Igloo Vikski Inc, 2016 SCC 38 at para 18). The reviewing court examines the decision for “the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process” and determines “whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47). These criteria are met if “the reasons allow the reviewing court to understand why the tribunal made its decision and permit it to determine whether the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes” (Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 16). The reviewing court should intervene only if these criteria are not met. It is not the role of the reviewing court to reweigh the evidence or to substitute its own view of a preferable outcome (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59 and 61).

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the reasonableness standard requiring justification, transparency, and acceptable outcomes without reweighing evidence.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the RPD's finding that the claim is clearly fraudulent and manifestly unfounded is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The sole issue raised by the applicant is whether the RPD’s determination that his claim for protection is clearly fraudulent and, therefore, manifestly unfounded is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant challenges the reasonableness of the RPD's finding that his claim is fraudulent and manifestly unfounded.

propositions.text: Section 107.1 of IRPA requires RPD to state claim is manifestly unfounded if claim is clearly fraudulent.
propositions.quote: Section 107.1 of the IRPA provides that, if the RPD rejects a claim for refugee protection, “it must state in its reasons for the decision that the claim is manifestly unfounded if it is of the opinion that the claim is clearly fraudulent.”

propositions.text: Claim is clearly fraudulent if decision maker has firm conviction claim is sought through fraudulent means affecting protection grant.
propositions.quote: A claim may be found to be clearly fraudulent when “the decision maker has the firm conviction that refugee protection is sought through fraudulent means, such as falsehoods or dishonest conduct that go to the determination of whether or not refugee protection will be granted” (Warsame v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 596 at para 31 [Warsame]).

propositions.text: Finding of fraud requires deliberate false portrayal of core claim matters, more than claim rejection.
propositions.quote: It requires more than simply the rejection of the claim. The decision maker must find that the claimant has deliberately portrayed matters that go to the core of the claim for protection falsely (Warsame at para 36).

propositions.text: Finding claim manifestly unfounded bars Refugee Appeal Division access; applicant barred anyway as claim predates RAD.
propositions.quote: While such a finding bars access to the Refugee Appeal Division (see section 110(2)(c) of the IRPA), the applicant is barred from access to this in any event because his claim pre-dates its establishment (see sections 36(1) and 37 of the Balanced Refugee Reform Act, SC 2010, c 8, as amended by the Protecting Canada’s Immigration System Act, SC 2012, c 17).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains section 107.1 IRPA requires manifestly unfounded finding if claim is clearly fraudulent, citing Warsame, and notes applicant barred from RAD.

propositions.text: Refugee claimant bears onus to establish essential claim elements; RPD may base decision on credible evidence.
propositions.quote: The onus rests on a refugee claimant to establish the essential elements of his or her claim for protection. The RPD “may receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered credible or trustworthy in the circumstances” (IRPA, s 170(h)).

propositions.text: Claimant not required to provide corroboration unless truthfulness is questioned; sworn allegations presumed true unless doubted.
propositions.quote: A claimant is not required to provide corroborative evidence unless there are valid reasons to question the claimant’s truthfulness. This is because, when a refugee claimant swears that certain allegations are true, the allegations are to be taken as true unless there is reason to doubt that this is so (Maldonado v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 FC 302 at para 5 (CA)[Maldonado]).

propositions.text: Presumption of truthfulness rebuttable by inconsistent evidence or credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: This presumption of truthfulness can be rebutted by evidence that is inconsistent with the claimant’s allegations. It can also be rebutted when there are grounds to find that the claimant’s testimony lacks credibility (Ismaili v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 84 at para 36; Guven v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 38 at paras 35-38).

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimant must prove essential elements; corroboration not required unless truthfulness questioned, citing Maldonado and other cases.

propositions.text: Credibility findings may be based on testimony manner but require care and sensitivity to claimant's circumstances.
propositions.quote: A finding that a claimant lacks credibility may be based on the manner in which the claimant testified at the hearing, although such determinations must always be made with care and sensitivity to the specific circumstances of the claimant (cf. Rozas Del Solar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 1145 at paras 102-04; R v N.S., 2012 SCC 72 at paras 21-27).

propositions.text: Credibility may also be based on failure of account to withstand scrutiny, including inconsistencies or contradictions.
propositions.quote: It may also be based on the failure of the claimant’s account to stand up to scrutiny, whether intrinsically or against extrinsic evidence such as country conditions. The implausibility of a claimant’s account, or unexplained inconsistencies, omissions, or contradictions, can lead to adverse credibility findings and the rejection of the claim.

propositions.text: Adverse credibility findings should not be based on microscopic evaluation of peripheral or irrelevant issues.
propositions.quote: Still, such findings should not be “based on a microscopic evaluation of issues peripheral or irrelevant to the case” (Haramichael v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1197 at para 15, citing Lubana v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FCT 116 at paras 10-11; Rahal at para 43).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains credibility findings may be based on testimony manner or inconsistencies but must avoid microscopic evaluation of irrelevant issues.

propositions.text: Corroborative evidence can bolster or restore confidence in claimant's truthfulness but is not generally required.
propositions.quote: Credible or trustworthy corroborative evidence can bolster one’s confidence in a claimant’s truthfulness (even though this may be unnecessary given the Maldonado presumption) or it can restore one’s confidence in the claimant’s truthfulness when this has been cast into doubt.

propositions.text: Panel errs if adverse credibility finding based solely on absence of corroborative evidence.
propositions.quote: There is no general requirement for corroboration and a panel errs if it makes an adverse credibility finding on the basis of the absence of corroborative evidence alone (Ndjavera v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 452 at para 6).

propositions.text: If truthfulness questioned, panel may consider failure to provide corroboration if claimant cannot reasonably explain absence.
propositions.quote: However, if there are valid reasons to question a claimant’s truthfulness, the panel may also consider the claimant’s failure to provide corroborative evidence, but only where the claimant could not give a reasonable explanation for the absence of such evidence (Dundar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 1026 at para 22, citing Amarapala v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 12 para 10).

paragraphs.summary: The court states corroboration can support truthfulness but is not required; absence alone cannot justify adverse credibility finding.

propositions.text: Corroborative evidence must be examined independently before rejection; cannot reject it solely because claimant lacks credibility.
propositions.quote: Even so, the evidence must be examined independently of concerns about the claimant’s credibility before it is rejected (Yu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1138 at paras 31-37; Lu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 846 at paras 33-35).

propositions.text: Rejecting corroborative evidence solely because claimant is not believed risks circular reasoning.
propositions.quote: Otherwise, the decision maker risks reasoning in a way that begs the very question at issue: the corroborative evidence is not believed simply because the claimant is not believed (Sterling v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 329 at para 12).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains corroborative evidence must be independently assessed and not rejected solely because claimant lacks credibility.

propositions.text: Member found applicant failed to establish he was a genuine Christian; applicant maintained he was but member disbelieved him.
propositions.quote: The member’s central finding in the present case was that the applicant had failed to establish that he was a genuine Christian. The applicant obviously maintained that he was but the member did not believe him.

propositions.text: Member's assessment of evidence meets reasonableness test in several respects but has a fatal flaw.
propositions.quote: In a number of respects, the member’s assessment of the evidence meets the test of reasonableness. However, as I will explain, it suffers from a fatal flaw.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member reasonably disbelieved the applicant's Christian claim but the assessment has a fatal flaw.

propositions.text: Member rejected applicant's evidence partly due to material differences in his accounts about China events.
propositions.quote: The member’s rejection of the applicant’s evidence about his Christian identity rested in part on material differences between the applicant’s accounts of what had happened in China.

propositions.text: Applicant disputes only the role of Mr. Xi in escape from PSB on judicial review.
propositions.quote: The only one of these that the applicant takes issue with on this application for judicial review is the role of Mr. Xi in the escape from the PSB.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel parses testimony too finely to explain omission of Mr. Xi earlier; member could consider omission in assessing claim.
propositions.quote: In my view, counsel for the applicant attempts to parse the applicant’s testimony before the RPD too finely to explain why he did not mention Mr. Xi earlier. In any event, it was open to the member to consider the omission of Mr. Xi in the first PIF and his inclusion in the second when assessing the applicant’s claim that the police raided a church service he was participating in on April 18, 2010, a pivotal event in his narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member reasonably considered material differences in applicant's accounts, including omission of Mr. Xi, despite applicant's dispute.

propositions.text: Member also rejected claim partly due to failure to produce corroborative documents about religious practices in China.
propositions.quote: The member’s rejection of the applicant’s claim also rested in part on the applicant’s failure to produce corroborative documents relating to his religious practices in China.

propositions.text: Given account differences, member reasonably asked why no evidence corroborating Christian practice in China was produced.
propositions.quote: Given the differences between the applicant’s accounts of material events, it was reasonable for the member to ask the applicant why he had not produced any evidence to corroborate his claim that he had been a practicing Christian in China, the central element of his claim for protection (Yu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 310 at para 28; He v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 525 at para 14; He v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 362 at para 22).

propositions.text: Applicant explained religious practices were secret, but member did not find explanation reasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant attempted to explain why he had not provided any such evidence – his religious practices had been secret at the time – but the member did not find this a reasonable explanation in the circumstances.

propositions.text: Member's conclusion rejecting explanation was open to him; crucially, no adverse inference drawn from absence of corroboration alone.
propositions.quote: In my view, this conclusion was open to the member. Crucially, the member did not draw an adverse inference from the absence of corroborative evidence alone.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member reasonably rejected applicant's explanation for lack of corroboration but did not draw adverse inference from absence alone.

propositions.text: Applicant relied on evidence of Christian practices in Canada to support claim and sur place claim.
propositions.quote: The applicant also relied on evidence of continuing Christian practices in Canada to support his claim to have been a Christian in China and to support his sur place claim.

propositions.text: RPD's assessment of this evidence is intelligible and justifiable; letters and evidence insufficient to establish genuineness given credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: Standing on its own, the RPD’s assessment of this evidence is intelligible and justifiable. It was open to the RPD to find that the letters from Reverend Ko and the other evidence were insufficient to establish the genuineness of the applicant’s claim to be a practicing Christian, particularly in light of the member’s concerns about the applicant’s credibility concerning the events in China (see, for example, Li v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 998 at paras 29 and 32, and Su at para 17).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD reasonably assessed Canadian Christian practice evidence as insufficient given credibility concerns about China events.

propositions.text: Applicant's claim required other corroboration to succeed; PSB documents were important but member's findings on them are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Given the foregoing, the applicant’s claim for protection required some other form of corroboration if it was to have any chance of success. The PSB documents could serve such a purpose, which is why they were an important element of the claim. In my view, however, the member’s findings concerning these documents are unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member's findings on PSB documents unreasonable despite their importance to the applicant's claim.

propositions.text: Member found PSB documents fraudulent because they do not comply with Chinese criminal procedure law.
propositions.quote: Rather, the member concluded that the documents were fraudulent because he found that the law of criminal procedure in China does not expressly provide for the use of such documents.

propositions.text: Member reasoned Wanted Circular not compliant with law and Release Certificates lacked legal basis, so must be fraudulent.
propositions.quote: The member reasoned that since the Wanted Circular “does not comply with” and “is not in keeping with” the law of Chinese criminal procedure, it must be fraudulent. Similarly, since the member could not find any reference to Release Certificates in the law of Chinese criminal procedure, and since the statutory provision referred to in the Release Certificates tendered by the applicant did not appear to have anything to do with the power to release someone upon the completion of a criminal sentence, these documents must be fraudulent as well.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the member's finding that PSB documents are fraudulent due to non-compliance with Chinese criminal procedure law.

propositions.text: Stronger evidence needed to reasonably conclude PSB documents are fraudulent; evidence did not exclude their use.
propositions.quote: In my view, a stronger evidentiary foundation is required to support a reasonable conclusion that these documents are fraudulent. The evidence before the member did not foreclose the possibility that such documents could be used.

propositions.text: Member's finding of fraud and manifestly unfounded claim determination are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In the absence of evidence that the PSB does not use such documents, whether as a matter of practice or because the law does not permit it, the member’s finding that the documents are fraudulent is unreasonable. The determination that the claim is manifestly unfounded is, therefore, also unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the member's fraud finding and manifestly unfounded determination unreasonable due to insufficient evidence about PSB documents.

propositions.text: Applicant submits error on Wanted Circular is determinative as it corroborates essential claim element.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that this error with respect to the Wanted Circular is determinative of the application for judicial review because, if the document is authentic, it corroborates an essential element of his claim.

propositions.text: Error in finding document fraudulent does not mean member erred in not accepting it as genuine.
propositions.quote: It does not follow from the fact that the member erred in finding that the document is fraudulent that the member therefore also erred in not accepting it as genuine.

propositions.text: PSB documents' probative value and weight not properly assessed by RPD.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, we are left with a potentially significant document whose probative value and weight have not been assessed properly by the RPD. This is also the case with respect to the Release Certificates.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues error on Wanted Circular is determinative; court finds RPD did not properly assess PSB documents' probative value.

propositions.text: Reasonable decision maker could find applicant's claim weak; rejection might withstand review if PSB documents properly considered.
propositions.quote: As discussed above, a reasonable decision maker could find that the applicant’s claim for protection suffers from a number of weaknesses. Other things being equal, the member’s rejection of the applicant’s claim could well have withstood review.

propositions.text: Court cannot determine if PSB documents overcome account frailties without proper RPD findings; new hearing required.
propositions.quote: This, however, is not for me to determine in the absence of findings by the RPD concerning those documents that are not tainted by reviewable errors. Given the centrality of the PSB documents to the applicant’s claim, I am unable to find that the decision overall is reasonable (cf. Ma v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 163 at para 19, and Nagornyak v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 215 at para 33). The applicant is entitled to a proper assessment of the significance of these documents by the RPD. There must, therefore, be a new hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claim weak but cannot decide without proper RPD findings on PSB documents; orders new hearing.

propositions.text: Judicial review application allowed; RPD decision set aside and matter remitted to differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The decision of the RPD dated December 5, 2017, is set aside and the matter is remitted for reconsideration by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review, sets aside RPD decision, and remits matter to a new panel.

propositions.text: No questions of general importance suggested or found for certification.
propositions.quote: The parties did not suggest any questions of general importance for certification. I agree that none arise.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no questions of general importance for certification.
